questions_and_answers.question_text: What does bú shi...jiù shi... mean?
What is the literal meaning of xī dú?
What two parts do Chinese verbs for "kill" often consist of?
What are the general and specific meanings of shā?
Which verb translates "make" when it means "to compel"?
Write the Chinese for "He killed that man with a gun."

answers.answer_text: Tā yòng qiāng bǎ nèige rén dǎsǐ le.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Why is Tā yòng qiāng bǎ nèige rén shāsǐ le wrong?

answers.answer_text: Because shā takes on its specific meaning (killing with a knife) as soon as a method is mentioned — with a gun you must use dǎsǐ.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Where does an aspect marker go in a shǐ sentence?

answers.answer_text: With the verb following shǐ, never with shǐ itself.

questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the most general Chinese verb for killing by any means?
Does shā always imply the victim died?

answers.answer_text: No — shā may express the action of only trying to kill.

articles.text:
8. A: Nǐ kàn, zhèipiān wénzhāngli    Look, there's nothing in this article
      bú shi xī dú, jiù shi shā rén. but taking drugs and killing people.
   B: Kàn zhèizhǒng xīnwén, zhǐ     Reading this kind of news will only make
      néng shǐ rén nánshòu. Suàn     you feel bad. Forget it, don't read it.
      le, bú yào kàn le.

Notes on No. 8

bú shi...jiù shi...: "if it's not...then it's..." or "EITHER...OR...."

Bú shi tā, jiù shi nǐ.           It was either he or you.
Lǎo Wáng zuò cài, bú shi tài     Lǎo Wáng's cooking is always either
xián jiù shi tài là.             too salty or too hot.
Tā bú shi zài jiā, jiù shi zài   If he isn't at home, then he's at the
bàngōngshì.                      office.

xī dú: "to take drugs." Literally "to inhale poison," but used for ANY method of drug taking.

shā rén: "to kill, to murder" — or "to TRY (unsuccessfully) to kill." The Chinese verbs for "kill" often consist of TWO parts: a verb telling the ACTION (stab, shoot, beat) and a verb telling the resulting PROCESS OF DYING:

hàisǐ (by scheming)          zhásǐ (by stabbing)
diànsǐ (by electric shock)   dúsǐ (by poisoning)
diàosǐ (by hanging)          mènsǐ (by suffocation or drowning)
lēisǐ (by strangling with a cord)   qiāsǐ (by strangling with the hands)
yāsǐ (by crushing or running over)  zhuàngsǐ (by a collision)
qìsǐ (by making someone angry!)     dǎsǐ (by a blow, beating, or gunshot)
and the most general term of all:   nòngsǐ (by any means)

In classical Chinese, shā originally meant "to kill WITH A KNIFE" or "to slaughter (an animal)." Today, shā is still used for slaughtering animals.

In modern Chinese, shā can have (1) a GENERAL meaning or (2) a SPECIFIC meaning.

(1) GENERAL — same as nòngsǐ or English "to kill, to murder." Used when the method is NOT stated or NOT known.

Tā bǎ nèige rén shāsǐ le.        He killed that person.

(2) SPECIFIC — to kill with a KNIFE or knifelike instrument. Shā takes on this specific meaning AS SOON AS you start talking about METHODS, so in such sentences you MUST choose your verb according to the mode of killing. It would be WRONG to say Tā yòng qiāng bǎ nèige rén shāsǐ le. Instead say:

Tā yòng qiāng bǎ nèige rén dǎsǐ  He killed that man with a gun.
le.

Shā may express the action of only TRYING to kill, without implying that the person or animal actually died.

shǐ: "to cause, to make"

shǐ rén nánshòu                  "makes one sad"
zhēn shǐ wǒ gāoxìng              "really makes me happy"
shǐ wǒ juéde yǒu xīwàng          "makes me feel that there's hope"

If there is an ASPECT MARKER, it goes with the verb FOLLOWING shǐ, NEVER with shǐ itself.

Shǐ sometimes means "TO ENABLE," particularly if followed by néng.

Although shǐ may sometimes be translated by "make," "make" may NOT always be translated by shǐ. When "make" means "TO COMPEL" someone to do something, use JIÀO:

Lǐ Xiānsheng jiào tā zài xiě     Mr. Lǐ made him write it over again.
yícì.
